title: The charnel ground
hookLine: monks once reflected on bodies left in the cemetery, and turned the reflection on themselves

lines: THEN LOOK AT YOUR OWN BODY.
cards: Bones, bleached white, the color of shells. That's one of the images in an old Buddhist discourse on the foundations of mindfulness.

It describes a charnel ground, an open field outside a town where bodies were left rather than buried, and asks a monk to sit with what happens there, stage by stage, then turn and look at his own body. It is a hard text.
Read slowly, it is also a strangely tender one, and it hands the monk one line to carry home.

teach.b: First, the stages. In the Satipatthana discourse, the Buddha describes a monk who sees, or calls to mind, a body thrown aside in a charnel ground: one, two or three days dead, swollen, discolored.
Then a body eaten by crows and dogs and jackals. Then a skeleton held together by sinews. Then bones scattered in every direction.
Then bones white as shells, bones in a heap, bones crumbling to dust. The text doesn't hurry. Second, the turn.
After each picture comes the same move.

teach.h: THIS BODY TOO IS OF THE SAME NATURE.
teach.b: The monk compares it with his own body: this body too is of the same nature, it will become like that, it is not exempt from that. The point is not disgust at someone else.
It is to see his own body plainly, as one of all bodies. Third, why a body.
In this discourse the reflection sits among other ways of attending to the body: the breath, and the postures of walking, standing, sitting and lying down.
It's mindfulness, not morbidity. Seeing the body as it is, Buddhists say, loosens clinging to it, and the fear that comes with that clinging. Fourth, taught gently.
Some teachers today still offer the cemetery reflection, by a walk among graves, by images, or simply in words.
Others set it aside for someone in fresh grief, or for someone with a hard history with their body.
The text is strong medicine, and like any strong medicine, it's given with care, in a dose a person can take.

how: In some Buddhist traditions, monastics and lay practitioners reflect on the body's impermanence using the charnel-ground contemplations, in words, images or cemetery visits, and teachers adapt or set them aside for people who are grieving.

games.q: you're a monk sitting at the charnel ground, looking at bones white as shells. what does the discourse ask you to do next?
o: leave quickly and think of something pleasant.
turn and see your own body: it is of the same nature.
pity the dead and feel glad you're alive.
games.why: each picture ends with the same turn: this body too is of the same nature, it will become like that, it is not exempt.

practice: Feel your body from the inside: the weight on the seat, the hands, the warmth of the chest, the breath moving, this body that has carried you all your life.
Then quietly add the discourse's line, this body too is of the same nature, not as a threat but as a fact you share with everyone you love and everyone you pass on the street.
If that's too heavy today, simply feel the body breathing and leave the line aside.

wordCard.voice: Satipatthana, the Buddhist discourse on mindfulness that asks a monk to see his own body as one of all bodies. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali, written in Devanagari: satipaṭṭhāna, the foundations of mindfulness, the discourse that holds the charnel-ground reflection.

carryVoice: Your line: all bodies. A stranger's body and yours share the same nature. Until tomorrow.
